Mate Rimac's Bugatti Got Stolen: He Found the Thief in Austria, Wanted To Give Him a Lift Home
12 photos
Photo: Mate Rimac | Instagram
Bugatti Rimac CEO Mate Rimac had his personal $3.3 million Bugatti Chiron stolen from the company's unfenced campus in Croatia. Rimac made one rookie mistake, overestimating the safety of the campus: he left the keys inside the vehicle and walked into his office. The thief was already on his way to Germany by the time the owner of the car realized it was gone. When he found his car, he wanted to give the man a lift home
A 36-year-old Croatian man wandering the campus looking for a job spotted the Bugatti Chiron parked with the keys inside. Security cameras caught the man finishing a cigarette before hopping in and driving off in broad daylight.
Because factory employees frequently move cars for testing and his Chiron is often driven around the campus by others, Mate Rimac always leaves it with the keys inside. So when he saw it was not parked where he had left it, he just assumed someone needed to move it. However, he was eventually told that a stranger drove off in his Chiron.
At this point, Mate Rimac called the police. Authorities reported the theft to neighboring countries. By that time, the thief and the car had already crossed the border. In the meantime, Mate Rimac did not just sit with his arms crossed, waiting for the police to solve the case. He used the Chiron's built-in advanced telemetry tracking system to pull up real-time live coordinates, speed metrics, and fuel level.
Photo: Mate Rimac | Instagram Once he got access to the real-time location, Rimac and his team set up a digital command center by launching a group chat that included local law enforcement. However, he was not going to just sit in his office and let the police chase the thief.
Mate got in his Porsche 911 Turbo S and started his own chase. He knew that the thief would not get very far with the gas he had left in the tank of the Chiron. He did stop for a refill and, as expected, left without paying. That was when his one-hour head start was reduced, while Rimac was pushing his Porsche to close the gap.
The telemetry showed the thief blazing past the Slovenian border and crossing straight into Austria. Rimac's team kept feeding data to the authorities. The Austrian police coordinated an interception strategy and cornered the thief along the A9 Pyhrn motorway near Graz.
Mate Rimac expected to just flash his ID, thank the officers, and drive his Bugatti back home to Croatia. Instead, he found about 10 police cars and 20 officers at the scene. Because the Chiron had been involved in an international theft and was worth millions, the Austrian police refused to simply hand it over on the side of the road.
Photo: Rimac Automobili Police ordered the Bugatti to be loaded onto a flatbed tow truck and moved to the local police precinct. So the owner had to follow the police caravan to the station and stay there until the early hours of the next morning, filling out international cross-border grand theft paperwork.
It was during this late-night stint at the precinct that Rimac asked to meet the thief face to face. What would have normally been a very heated confrontation turned into a remarkably calm conversation.
He found out that the 36-year-old suspect was coming from a very difficult background and had originally walked into the unfenced Bugatti campus to ask for a job, but when he saw the Chiron and noticed it had the keys in, he just couldn't help himself.
The Bugatti CEO recalled with a bit of amusement that the thief framed it " like it was my faul t" for tempting him with an open car. He confessed that he had no grand black-market smuggling operation plans. He simply panicked, put his foot down, and headed for Germany for completely unknown reasons.
Photo: Mate Rimac | Instagram Rimac explained that he leaves his cars unlocked all the time because Croatia is incredibly safe. Regardless of the country's crime rate, he will probably think twice when he gets out of the car and walks away.
Impressed by the man's story, state of mind, and family situation, Mate Rimac decided not to press charges and said he would have gladly picked the man up and driven him back home to his family himself. However, the case is completely out of his hands. Public prosecutors in Graz, Austria, and the Croatian police are moving forward with criminal prosecution.
The Bugatti Chiron sustained some minor damage to its front end during the multi-country getaway. Rimac brushed it off on social media, saying, " I don't care, we will repair it, " says the man who occaasionally drives a Volkswagen Golf R32 . A new front spoiler for the CEO of a company that builds hypercars is not exactly something to worry about.
Don't be surprised if Mate Rimac calls the man for an interview and hires him at Bugatti. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mate Rimac (@materimac)
